question: Which class of criminal courts in CrPC 1973 has been completely eliminated in the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS)?
options: Metropolitan Magistrates
Judicial Magistrates of the First Class
Courts of Session
Executive Magistrates
explanation: BNSS Section 6 abolishes the separate cadre of Metropolitan Magistrates; throughout India only Judicial Magistrates (JMFC/JMIC) and Executive Magistrates are retained under Courts of Session.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Metropolitan Magistrates are omitted in BNSS Section 6.
optionBreakdown.C: Retained as principal trial court of district.

learningObjective: Master elimination of Metropolitan Magistrates in BNSS.

question: How many classes of Criminal Courts (besides High Courts and special courts) are established under Section 6 BNSS?
options: Four classes: Court of Session, JMFC, JMIC, and Executive Magistrates
Two classes only
Five classes including Metropolitan Magistrates
Three classes
explanation: Section 6 BNSS specifies four classes: (i) Courts of Session; (ii) Judicial Magistrates of the first class; (iii) Judicial Magistrates of the second class; (iv) Executive Magistrates.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; exactly four classes under Section 6 BNSS.

learningObjective: Recall four classes of criminal courts.

question: Under Section 8 BNSS (Section 9 CrPC), who establishes the Court of Session for every sessions division?
options: The State Government, but the High Court appoints the Judge
The High Court exclusively
The Governor with approval of President
The Chief Judicial Magistrate
explanation: The State Government establishes a Court of Session for every sessions division, but the Judge thereof is appointed by the High Court.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; established by State Govt, Judge appointed by High Court.
optionBreakdown.B: High Court appoints judges, does not establish the territorial court itself.
optionBreakdown.D: CJM is subordinate to Sessions Judge.

learningObjective: Distinguish role of State Govt and High Court in Sessions Courts.

question: Who appoints the Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM) in every district under Section 9 BNSS (Section 12 CrPC)?
options: The High Court
The State Government
The Sessions Judge
The District Magistrate
explanation: Section 9(1) BNSS (Section 12(1) CrPC) provides that in every district the High Court shall appoint a Judicial Magistrate of the first class to be the Chief Judicial Magistrate.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; CJM is appointed by High Court from JMFCs.
optionBreakdown.B: State Government does not appoint judicial magistrates.
optionBreakdown.C: Sessions Judge exercises supervisory power, not appointment.
optionBreakdown.D: District Magistrate is head of Executive Magistrates.

learningObjective: Recall authority appointing CJM.

question: To whom is the Chief Judicial Magistrate subordinate under Section 12 BNSS (Section 15 CrPC)?
options: Subordinate to the Sessions Judge
Subordinate to the District Magistrate
Subordinate directly to the Chief Minister
Subordinate to the Director of Prosecution
explanation: Section 12(1) BNSS (Section 15(1) CrPC) mandates that every Chief Judicial Magistrate shall be subordinate to the Sessions Judge.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; CJM is subordinate to the Sessions Judge.
optionBreakdown.B: Judicial Magistrates are completely independent of DM under separation of powers.

learningObjective: Understand judicial hierarchy and subordination of CJM.

question: Who appoints Special Judicial Magistrates under Section 11 BNSS (Section 13 CrPC)?
options: The High Court, upon request of Central or State Government
The Governor directly
The Law Minister
The Supreme Court Collegium
explanation: The High Court may, if requested by Central or State Government, confer upon any qualified person the powers of a JMFC or JMIC as Special Judicial Magistrate for up to 1 year at a time.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; High Court upon request of Central/State Govt.
optionBreakdown.B: Governor does not appoint judicial magistrates.

learningObjective: Recall Special Judicial Magistrate appointment provisions.

question: Under Section 14 BNSS (Section 20 CrPC), who appoints Executive Magistrates in every district?
options: The State Government, and appoints one of them to be the District Magistrate
The High Court
The Sessions Judge
The Central Home Ministry
explanation: The State Government appoints in every district as many persons as it thinks fit to be Executive Magistrates, and appoints one to be District Magistrate.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; State Government appoints Executive Magistrates.

learningObjective: Identify appointment authority for Executive Magistrates.

question: Can an Additional Sessions Judge try cases directly without an order of committal or transfer from the Sessions Judge?
options: No; an Additional Sessions Judge tries only cases made over by general or special order of the Sessions Judge or High Court
Yes, has concurrent direct original filing jurisdiction
Yes, in all non-bailable cases
Only on Sundays
explanation: Under Section 8(3) BNSS / S. 9(3) CrPC, an Additional Sessions Judge exercises jurisdiction only over cases made over by the Sessions Judge or directed by High Court.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Additional Sessions Judge tries made-over cases.
optionBreakdown.B: Direct filing is in Court of Session under Sessions Judge.

learningObjective: Master Additional Sessions Judge jurisdiction.

question: In which landmark case did the Supreme Court enforce separation of the judiciary from the executive under Article 50 across subordinate criminal courts?
options: State of Bihar v. Bal Mukund Sah (2000)
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950)
explanation: Bal Mukund Sah ((2000) 4 SCC 640) reaffirmed that subordinate criminal judiciary is under the exclusive control of the High Court pursuant to Article 50 and 235.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Bal Mukund Sah on separation of subordinate criminal courts.
optionBreakdown.C: Procedure established by law under Art 21.

provision: BNSS S. 6 / Art. 50 / Bal Mukund Sah
learningObjective: Understand constitutional separation in criminal judiciary.

question: Under Section 7 BNSS (Section 7 CrPC), every State shall be a sessions division or consist of sessions divisions, and every sessions division shall be:
options: A district or consist of districts
A police station
A subdivision only
A municipality
explanation: Section 7 BNSS mandates that every State shall be a sessions division or consist of sessions divisions; and every sessions division shall, for the purposes of this Sanhita, be a district or consist of districts.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; sessions division is a district or consists of districts.
optionBreakdown.B: Police station is an investigation unit.

learningObjective: Define territorial units of criminal administration.

question: Under Section 22(2) BNSS (Section 28(2) CrPC), what sentences may a Sessions Judge or Additional Sessions Judge pass?
options: Any sentence authorised by law, but any sentence of death passed by any such Judge shall be subject to confirmation by the High Court
Any sentence except death
Imprisonment up to 10 years only
Any sentence without requiring confirmation
explanation: A Sessions Judge or Additional Sessions Judge may pass any sentence authorised by law, but a death sentence requires confirmation by High Court under Chapter 30 (S. 407 BNSS / S. 366 CrPC).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; any sentence, but death requires High Court confirmation.
optionBreakdown.B: Sessions Judge CAN pass death sentence, subject to confirmation.
optionBreakdown.C: 10 years applies to Assistant Sessions Judge in CrPC.

learningObjective: Recall Sessions Court sentencing jurisdiction.

question: What significant change has BNSS 2023 made regarding Assistant Sessions Judges?
options: The post and sentencing jurisdiction of Assistant Sessions Judge (formerly S. 28(3) CrPC: up to 10 years) has been abolished in BNSS
Assistant Sessions Judges can now pass death sentences
Assistant Sessions Judges are renamed Chief Magistrates
Assistant Sessions Judges are transferred to civil courts
explanation: BNSS Section 22 completely eliminates Assistant Sessions Judges; only Sessions Judges and Additional Sessions Judges are retained at the Sessions level.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Assistant Sessions Judge post is omitted in BNSS.

learningObjective: Master abolition of Assistant Sessions Judge in BNSS.

question: What sentence may the Court of a Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM) pass under Section 23(1) BNSS (Section 29(1) CrPC)?
options: Any sentence authorised by law except a sentence of death or of imprisonment for life or of imprisonment for a term exceeding seven years
Imprisonment up to 3 years and fine up to Rs 50,000
Imprisonment up to 10 years
Any sentence authorised by law without restriction
explanation: Section 23(1) BNSS (Section 29(1) CrPC) provides that a CJM may pass any sentence except death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment exceeding 7 years.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; up to 7 years imprisonment (cannot pass death/life/7+ yrs).

learningObjective: Recall sentencing power of CJM.

question: What are the sentencing powers of a Judicial Magistrate First Class (JMFC) under Section 23(2) BNSS (Section 29(2) CrPC)?
options: Imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or fine not exceeding Rs 50,000, or both, or community service
Imprisonment up to 1 year and fine up to Rs 5,000
Imprisonment up to 7 years
Imprisonment up to 3 years and fine up to Rs 10,000
explanation: Section 23(2) BNSS increased the maximum fine for JMFC from Rs 10,000 (under CrPC) to Rs 50,000, and added community service as a sentencing option.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; up to 3 years, fine up to Rs 50,000, or community service.
optionBreakdown.D: Rs 10,000 was the old CrPC limit.

learningObjective: Master enhanced JMFC fine limit (Rs 50,000) under BNSS.

question: What are the sentencing powers of a Judicial Magistrate Second Class (JMIC) under Section 23(3) BNSS (Section 29(3) CrPC)?
options: Imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year, or fine not exceeding Rs 10,000, or both, or community service
Imprisonment up to 3 years and fine up to Rs 50,000
Imprisonment up to 6 months only
Fine not exceeding Rs 1,000 only
explanation: Section 23(3) BNSS increased the maximum fine for JMIC from Rs 5,000 to Rs 10,000, with imprisonment up to 1 year and community service.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; up to 1 year, fine up to Rs 10,000, or community service.

learningObjective: Master enhanced JMIC fine limit (Rs 10,000) under BNSS.

question: Under Section 24 BNSS (Section 30 CrPC), what is the maximum imprisonment in default of payment of fine that a Magistrate may award?
options: Not exceed one-fourth of the maximum term of imprisonment which the Magistrate is competent to inflict for the offence
Not exceed one-half of the substantive sentence
Equal to the full substantive sentence
Maximum 14 days in all cases
explanation: Section 24(1)(b) BNSS / S. 30(1)(b) CrPC mandates that default imprisonment shall not exceed 1/4th of the maximum term the Magistrate is competent to inflict.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; not exceed 1/4th of the competent imprisonment term.

learningObjective: Apply one-fourth default imprisonment rule.

question: Can the term of imprisonment in default of fine be in addition to a substantive sentence of the maximum term awarded by the Magistrate?
options: Yes, under Section 24(2) BNSS / S. 30(2) CrPC, default imprisonment may be in addition to substantive imprisonment of the maximum term competent
No, total imprisonment can never exceed the maximum jurisdiction
Only if the High Court permits
Only in warrant trials
explanation: Section 24(2) BNSS (Section 30(2) CrPC) expressly states that the imprisonment awarded in default of fine may be in addition to a substantive sentence of the maximum term.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; default imprisonment is in addition to substantive sentence.
optionBreakdown.B: Default imprisonment does not merge with substantive ceiling.
optionBreakdown.C: Statutory rule does not require case-by-case HC permission.

learningObjective: Master default imprisonment additivity principle.

question: Under Section 25 BNSS (Section 31 CrPC), when a person is convicted at one trial of two or more offences, what is the aggregate limit of consecutive sentences that a Magistrate may impose?
options: Shall not exceed twice the amount of punishment which the Magistrate is competent to inflict for a single offence, nor exceed 14 years in aggregate
Shall not exceed 3 years
Shall not exceed 7 years
No aggregate ceiling exists
explanation: Section 25(2) BNSS / S. 31(2) CrPC limits aggregate consecutive sentences: not exceeding twice the competent jurisdiction, and maximum 14 years.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; twice the competent limit and maximum 14 years.

learningObjective: Master consecutive sentencing limits under S. 31 CrPC / S. 25 BNSS.

question: Under Section 407 BNSS (Section 366 CrPC), when a Court of Session passes a sentence of death:
options: The proceedings shall be submitted to the High Court, and the sentence shall not be executed unless confirmed by the High Court
The convict is executed within 30 days unless he appeals
The Governor must confirm within 60 days
Execution proceeds automatically unless stayed by Supreme Court
explanation: Section 407 BNSS (Section 366 CrPC) mandates that death sentence proceedings must be submitted to the High Court and cannot be executed until confirmed.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; mandatory High Court confirmation.
optionBreakdown.C: Governor acts under Art 161 (clemency), not statutory confirmation.

learningObjective: Recall death confirmation procedure.

question: How many Judges of the High Court must sign a confirmation of death sentence under Section 410 BNSS (Section 369 CrPC)?
options: At least two Judges
A Single Judge is competent
All Judges of the Full Bench
A Bench of three Judges
explanation: Section 410 BNSS (Section 369 CrPC) requires that confirmation or new sentence shall be made, passed and signed by at least two Judges when the High Court consists of two or more Judges.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; at least two Judges must hear and sign.
optionBreakdown.B: Single Judge cannot confirm capital sentence.
optionBreakdown.D: Three judges required only on split bench reference (S. 370).

learningObjective: Verify two-judge quorum for death confirmation.

question: Under Section 18 BNSS (Section 24 CrPC), how many years of practice as an advocate is mandatory for appointment as a Public Prosecutor or Additional Public Prosecutor?
options: Not less than seven years
Not less than five years
Not less than ten years
Not less than three years
explanation: Section 18(7) BNSS / S. 24(7) CrPC requires not less than 7 years of practice as an advocate for PP or Additional PP.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; not less than 7 years.
optionBreakdown.C: 10 years is required for Special Public Prosecutor.

learningObjective: Recall advocate experience for Public Prosecutor.

question: What is the minimum practice required for appointment as a Special Public Prosecutor under Section 18(8) BNSS (Section 24(8) CrPC)?
options: Not less than ten years as an advocate
Not less than seven years
Not less than fifteen years
Not less than five years
explanation: Section 18(8) BNSS (Section 24(8) CrPC) mandates not less than 10 years of practice as an advocate for Special Public Prosecutor.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; not less than 10 years.

learningObjective: Recall experience for Special Public Prosecutor.

question: Under Section 20 BNSS (Section 25A CrPC), who heads the Directorate of Prosecution in a State?
options: Director of Prosecution, who shall be a person who has been an advocate for not less than 15 years or a Sessions Judge
The Advocate General ex officio
The Director General of Police
The Chief Secretary
explanation: Section 20(2) BNSS provides that a person shall be eligible to be appointed as Director of Prosecution only if he has been in practice as an advocate for not less than 15 years or is or has been a Sessions Judge.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; advocate for 15+ years or Sessions Judge.
optionBreakdown.B: Advocate General is constitutional advisor under Art 165.

learningObjective: Recall qualifications for Director of Prosecution.

question: Who appoints Assistant Public Prosecutors (APPs) for conducting prosecutions in the Courts of Magistrates under Section 19 BNSS (Section 25 CrPC)?
options: The State Government
The High Court
The Sessions Judge
The Superintendent of Police
explanation: Section 19(1) BNSS (Section 25(1) CrPC) provides that the State Government shall appoint in every district one or more Assistant Public Prosecutors for conducting prosecution in Magistrate courts.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; appointed by State Government.
optionBreakdown.B: High Court does not appoint prosecutors.
optionBreakdown.C: Sessions Judge does not appoint prosecutors.

learningObjective: Recall appointment authority for Assistant Public Prosecutors.

question: Can a police officer be appointed as an Assistant Public Prosecutor under Section 19 BNSS (Section 25 CrPC)?
options: No police officer shall be eligible if he has taken any part in the investigation into the offence, or is below the rank of Inspector
Yes, any police constable can prosecute
Yes, the Investigating Officer must always prosecute
Police officers are absolutely barred under all circumstances
explanation: Under S. 19(2)-(3) BNSS / S. 25(2)-(3) CrPC, a police officer cannot be appointed if below the rank of Inspector or if he has taken part in the investigation of the offence.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; barred if investigated the offence or below Inspector rank.
optionBreakdown.C: IO cannot prosecute his own case (conflict of interest).
optionBreakdown.D: Ad hoc appointment permitted if above Inspector and not investigated.

learningObjective: Master police officer appointment restrictions as APP.

question: In Sheonandan Paswan v. State of Bihar ((1987) 1 SCC 288), what was held regarding the role of the Public Prosecutor under Section 321 CrPC (Section 360 BNSS)?
options: The Public Prosecutor is an officer of the court and a minister of justice; withdrawal from prosecution must be based on his independent executive judgment, not mere political dictation
Public Prosecutor is a mere mouthpiece of the ruling government
Court must mechanically grant withdrawal whenever requested
Only the victim can decide withdrawal
explanation: Sheonandan Paswan established that the Public Prosecutor is a minister of justice who must exercise independent discretion free from executive coercion.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; independent minister of justice exercising independent discretion.

provision: BNSS S. 360 / CrPC S. 321 / Sheonandan Paswan
learningObjective: Master Public Prosecutor independence doctrine.

question: To whom is the Directorate of Prosecution administratively subordinate under Section 20(3) BNSS (Section 25A(3) CrPC)?
options: The administrative head of the Home Department of the State
The Director General of Police
The High Court Registrar General
The Law Commission of India
explanation: Section 20(3) BNSS / S. 25A(3) CrPC specifies that the Head of the Directorate of Prosecution shall function under the administrative control of the Head of the Home Department in the State.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; functions under the Head of the Home Department.

learningObjective: Identify administrative control of Directorate of Prosecution.

question: Under Section 18(4) BNSS (Section 24(4) CrPC), the District Magistrate prepares a panel of names of persons fit to be appointed as Public Prosecutors in consultation with:
options: The Sessions Judge
The Superintendent of Police
The Chief Judicial Magistrate
The Bar Council Chairman
explanation: Section 18(4) BNSS / S. 24(4) CrPC provides that the District Magistrate shall, in consultation with the Sessions Judge, prepare a panel of names.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; in consultation with the Sessions Judge.
optionBreakdown.B: SP is not the statutory consultee.
optionBreakdown.D: Bar Council not involved in district panel.

learningObjective: Recall consultation authority for Public Prosecutor panel.

question: In Shiv Kumar v. Hukam Chand ((1999) 7 SCC 467), what did the Supreme Court hold regarding the role of a private counsel engaged by a complainant?
options: Private counsel must act under the directions of the Public Prosecutor and can only submit written arguments after evidence is closed with court permission
Private counsel can take over conduct of prosecution completely
Public Prosecutor must follow private counsel's instructions
Private counsel has equal standing with Public Prosecutor
explanation: Shiv Kumar settled that private counsel engaged by victim acts in subordinate capacity under the Public Prosecutor under S. 301/302 CrPC (S. 338/339 BNSS).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; acts subordinate to Public Prosecutor and submits written arguments.
optionBreakdown.B: Cannot supersede Public Prosecutor in Sessions Court.

learningObjective: Understand subordinate role of private counsel.

question: Under Section 18(1) BNSS, who appoints Public Prosecutors for the High Court?
options: The Central Government or the State Government, after consultation with the High Court
The Chief Justice of the High Court alone
The Union Law Minister
The Governor without consultation
explanation: Section 18(1) BNSS mandates that Central or State Government shall, after consultation with the High Court, appoint Public Prosecutors for the High Court.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Central or State Govt after consultation with High Court.
optionBreakdown.B: Chief Justice does not appoint directly.

learningObjective: Recall High Court Public Prosecutor appointment rules.

question: Under Section 35(1) BNSS (Section 41(1) CrPC), when can a police officer arrest without warrant a person against whom a reasonable complaint is made for an offence punishable up to 7 years?
options: Only if the police officer has reason to believe on the basis of such complaint that such person has committed the offence AND satisfies one of the specific necessity conditions (preventing further offence, proper investigation, tampering, absconding)
Automatically upon registration of any cognizable FIR
Whenever requested by the complainant in writing
Only after obtaining sanction from the High Court
explanation: Section 35(1)(b) BNSS / S. 41(1)(b) CrPC bars routine arrest for offences up to 7 years unless specific necessity criteria (a to e) are satisfied and recorded in writing.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; necessity conditions must be satisfied and recorded.
optionBreakdown.C: Complainant request does not justify arrest.
optionBreakdown.D: Sanction from High Court not required.

learningObjective: Master conditional arrest rule for offences up to 7 years.

question: What did the Supreme Court hold in the landmark decision of Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar ((2014) 8 SCC 273)?
options: Police officers must not arrest accused unnecessarily and Magistrates must not authorize detention mechanically; failure to comply with S. 41/41A attracts departmental action and contempt of court
Arrest is mandatory in all Section 498A IPC cases
Anticipatory bail is abolished for matrimonial offences
Police can detain suspects for 15 days without recording reasons
explanation: Arnesh Kumar issued mandatory directions to prevent unnecessary arrests in offences punishable up to 7 years, enforcing checklist and magistrate scrutiny.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Arnesh Kumar mandatory arrest guidelines and contempt consequences.

learningObjective: Master Arnesh Kumar arrest guidelines.

question: Under Section 35(3) BNSS (Section 41A CrPC), when the arrest of a person is not required under sub-section (1), what must the police officer issue?
options: A notice directing the person to appear before him or at such other place as may be specified
A non-bailable warrant
A proclamation under Section 82
An order of attachment
explanation: Section 35(3) BNSS (Section 41A CrPC) mandates issuing a Notice of Appearance where arrest is not necessary under Section 35(1).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Notice of Appearance under S. 35(3) BNSS / S. 41A CrPC.
optionBreakdown.B: Warrants are issued by courts, not police.

learningObjective: Define Notice of Appearance.

question: If a person complies with and continues to comply with a notice of appearance issued under Section 35(3) BNSS (Section 41A CrPC):
options: He shall not be arrested in respect of the offence referred to in the notice unless, for reasons to be recorded, the police officer is of the opinion that he ought to be arrested
He can still be arrested mechanically without recording reasons
He must deposit cash security of Rs 50,000
He is immune from prosecution permanently
explanation: Section 35(4) BNSS / S. 41A(3) CrPC confers statutory protection: person complying with notice shall not be arrested unless police record special reasons.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; cannot be arrested unless reasons recorded.
optionBreakdown.D: Immunity from arrest does not mean immunity from prosecution.

learningObjective: Understand protection afforded by compliance with S. 41A notice.

question: In Satender Kumar Antil v. CBI ((2022) 10 SCC 51), what did the Supreme Court hold regarding non-compliance with Section 41 and 41A CrPC?
options: Non-compliance entitles the accused to bail as a matter of right, and courts must enforce strict adherence to arrest safeguards
Non-compliance is a minor irregularity having no effect on bail
Arrest without notice is valid if the accused is wealthy
Section 41A is merely directory, not mandatory
explanation: Satender Kumar Antil categorized offences and held that non-compliance with S. 41/41A directly entitles the accused to bail.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; violation entitles accused to bail.

learningObjective: Master Satender Kumar Antil bail doctrine.

question: What new safeguard does Section 35(7) BNSS introduce regarding arrest of elderly persons or persons suffering from infirmity?
options: No arrest shall be made without prior permission of an officer not below Deputy Superintendent of Police where offence is punishable with less than 3 years and person is infirm or above 60 years
Complete immunity from trial
Trial can only be conducted at home
Arrest requires Presidential assent
explanation: Section 35(7) BNSS introduces a crucial new reform: for offences under 3 years, if person is infirm or over 60, arrest requires prior DSP permission.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; DSP permission required for elderly/infirm in petty offences.

learningObjective: Master elderly/infirm arrest safeguard in BNSS S. 35(7).

question: Can a private person arrest any person under Section 40 BNSS (Section 43 CrPC)?
options: Yes, if any person in his presence commits a non-bailable and cognizable offence, or is a proclaimed offender
Yes, for any civil default
Yes, whenever a private person suspects an offence
Private persons have no legal right to arrest
explanation: Section 40 BNSS (Section 43 CrPC) empowers any private person to arrest who in his presence commits a non-bailable and cognizable offence, or is a proclaimed offender.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; non-bailable & cognizable committed in his presence, or proclaimed offender.
optionBreakdown.C: Mere suspicion insufficient for private arrest.

learningObjective: Master private person arrest powers.

question: What must a private person do immediately after arresting an offender under Section 40(1) BNSS (Section 43(1) CrPC)?
options: Without unnecessary delay, make over the person to a police officer, or take him to the nearest police station
Interrogate the suspect at his home
Confiscate his mobile phone and money
Keep him detained until he confesses
explanation: Section 40(1) BNSS requires the private person to hand over the arrested person to a police officer or nearest police station without unnecessary delay.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; hand over without unnecessary delay to police.

learningObjective: Recall duty of private person post-arrest.

question: Under Section 41 BNSS (Section 44 CrPC), an Executive or Judicial Magistrate may arrest or order arrest of any person when:
options: Any offence is committed in the presence of the Magistrate within his local jurisdiction
An offence is committed anywhere in India
A anonymous complaint is received by telephone
The person is acquitted by a Sessions Court
explanation: Section 41(1) BNSS (Section 44(1) CrPC) allows a Magistrate to arrest or order arrest when any offence is committed in his presence within his local jurisdiction.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; offence committed in his presence within local jurisdiction.

learningObjective: Define Magistrate power of arrest under S. 44 CrPC / S. 41 BNSS.

question: Under Section 35(1)(c) BNSS, a person who has been proclaimed as an offender can be arrested by:
options: Any police officer without an order from a Magistrate and without a warrant
Only the CBI
Only the Sessions Judge personally
Only a police officer above SP rank
explanation: Section 35(1)(c) BNSS empowers any police officer to arrest a proclaimed offender without warrant.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; any police officer can arrest a proclaimed offender.

learningObjective: Recognize proclaimed offender arrest authority.

question: Which groundbreaking statutory provision is introduced in Section 43(3) BNSS regarding the use of handcuffs?
options: Codifies specific circumstances where police may use handcuffs (habitual/repeat offenders, escaped convicts, offences like terrorism, murder, rape, acid attack, organised crime)
Handcuffs are banned entirely in all circumstances
Police may handcuff any arrested person at their sole discretion
Handcuffs can only be used on women
explanation: Section 43(3) BNSS provides statutory codification for handcuffs: permitted for habitual offenders, escapees, or grave offences (rape, murder, terrorism, drugs, organised crime).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Section 43(3) BNSS codifies specific handcuff grounds.
optionBreakdown.B: Not totally banned under BNSS S. 43(3).
optionBreakdown.C: Discretion is circumscribed by statutory list.

learningObjective: Master statutory handcuffing rules under BNSS S. 43(3).

question: In Prem Shankar Shukla v. Delhi Administration ((1980) 3 SCC 526) and Citizen for Democracy (1995), what did the Supreme Court hold regarding handcuffing?
options: Handcuffing is prima facie inhuman, unreasonable and violative of Article 21; can only be justified if there is clear, present risk of escape or violence recorded in writing
Handcuffs should be applied to all undertrials as routine safety
Every accused must be chained during transport
Judicial permission is never required for handcuffs
explanation: Prem Shankar Shukla held that routine handcuffing violates human dignity under Art 21; special reasons must be recorded and judicial approval obtained.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; leading constitutional authority on handcuff restraint.

learningObjective: Analyze constitutional jurisprudence on handcuffing.

question: Under the Proviso to Section 43(1) BNSS (Section 46(1) CrPC), how must the arrest of a female be made?
options: Her submission to custody on oral intimation shall be presumed, and unless circumstances otherwise require or officer is female, police officer shall not touch her person
She must be handcuffed immediately
Arrest can be made by male officers without any female officer present
She must be searched in public
explanation: Proviso to S. 43(1) BNSS / S. 46(1) CrPC mandates that male police officers shall not touch the person of a woman for making arrest; custody is presumed on oral intimation.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; male officers cannot touch female arrestee; submission presumed.

learningObjective: Recall procedure for arrest of a female.

question: Under Section 43(5) BNSS (Section 46(4) CrPC), what is the statutory bar regarding arrest of women between sunset and sunrise?
options: No woman shall be arrested after sunset and before sunrise, save in exceptional circumstances and with prior permission of Judicial Magistrate First Class
No woman can ever be arrested at night under any circumstance
Police can arrest women at night if accompanied by two male witnesses
Arrest at night requires permission of the Superintendent of Police only
explanation: Section 43(5) BNSS (Section 46(4) CrPC) prohibits night arrest of women without prior written permission of Judicial Magistrate First Class.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; prior permission of JMFC required in exceptional circumstances.
optionBreakdown.B: Exceptional window with JMFC permission exists.
optionBreakdown.C: Requires JMFC order, not merely male witnesses.

learningObjective: Master sunset-sunrise female arrest rule.

question: Under Section 49 BNSS (Section 51 CrPC), whenever a female is to be searched, the search shall be made by:
options: Another female with strict regard to decency
Any police officer in presence of a Magistrate
A medical officer only
A male officer in presence of two women
explanation: Section 49(2) BNSS / S. 51(2) CrPC requires that whenever a female is searched, search shall be made by another female with strict regard to decency.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; search of female must be by female with strict decency.
optionBreakdown.C: Medical officer is for examination under S. 51 BNSS / S. 53 CrPC.

learningObjective: Recall female search safeguards.

question: Under Section 53 BNSS (Section 54 CrPC), medical examination of an arrested person by a medical officer immediately after arrest is:
options: Mandatory for every arrested person
Conducted only if the accused requests it in writing
Conducted only in murder cases
Conducted only if ordered by High Court
explanation: Section 53 BNSS (Section 54 CrPC) mandates medical examination of every arrested person immediately after arrest by a medical officer.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; mandatory examination of every arrestee.
optionBreakdown.B: Mandatory by law, not dependent on accused's request.
optionBreakdown.D: Statutory duty of police, no court order needed.

learningObjective: Master mandatory medical examination post-arrest.

question: Under Section 36 BNSS (Section 41B CrPC), every police officer making an arrest shall prepare a memorandum of arrest which shall be:
options: Attested by at least one witness who is a member of the family of the arrestee or a respectable member of the locality, and countersigned by the arrestee
Signed only by the police officer
Submitted to the High Court within 2 hours
Published in a local newspaper
explanation: Section 36 BNSS (Section 41B CrPC) requires memo of arrest attested by at least one witness (family member or locality resident) and countersigned by arrestee.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; statutory requirements of arrest memo.
optionBreakdown.B: Must be attested by independent/family witness.

learningObjective: Recall arrest memo requirements.

question: Under Section 43(2) BNSS (Section 46(2) CrPC), does the right to use all means necessary to effect arrest extend to causing death of the person?
options: No, nothing gives a right to cause death of a person who is not accused of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life
Yes, police can cause death of any fleeing suspect
Yes, in all non-bailable offences
Only if the suspect is a proclaimed offender
explanation: Section 43(2) Proviso BNSS / S. 46(3) CrPC explicitly bars causing death unless the person is accused of an offence punishable with death or life imprisonment.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; death can only be caused if offence carries death or life imprisonment.

learningObjective: Master statutory limitation on use of lethal force during arrest.

question: Under Section 50 BNSS (Section 52 CrPC), what power does a police officer have regarding offensive weapons found on an arrested person?
options: May seize all offensive weapons and shall deliver all weapons so taken to the Court or officer before whom the arrested person is required to be produced
May sell the weapons at public auction
Must return the weapons to the arrestee's family immediately
Can destroy the weapons on the spot
explanation: Section 50 BNSS (Section 52 CrPC) empowers the arresting officer to seize all offensive weapons and deliver them to the court or officer before whom arrestee is produced.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; seize and deliver to court/officer.
optionBreakdown.D: Weapons are case property and cannot be destroyed on the spot.

learningObjective: Recall weapon seizure procedure.

question: Under Section 51 BNSS (Section 53 CrPC), examination of an accused for rape or sexual offences (DNA profiling, swab collection) can be conducted by:
options: A registered medical practitioner at the request of a police officer not below the rank of Sub-Inspector
Any compounder or nurse
The Station House Officer himself
Only after the accused signs written consent
explanation: Section 51 BNSS / S. 53A CrPC provides that examination of person accused of rape shall be made by a registered medical practitioner on request of police officer not below Sub-Inspector.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; registered doctor on request of SI or above.
optionBreakdown.D: Reasonable force may be used; accused cannot veto examination.

learningObjective: Recall medical examination of rape accused.

question: Under Section 58 BNSS (Section 57 CrPC) and Article 22(2) of the Constitution, what is the maximum period an arrested person can be detained in police custody without production before a Magistrate?
options: Twenty-four hours exclusive of the time necessary for the journey from place of arrest to the Magistrate
Twenty-four hours inclusive of journey time
Forty-eight hours
Seventy-two hours
explanation: Section 58 BNSS, Section 57 CrPC, and Article 22(2) Constitution mandate production within 24 hours exclusive of journey time.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; 24 hours exclusive of journey time.

learningObjective: Recall 24-hour production rule.

question: In which landmark case did the Supreme Court lay down 11 mandatory guidelines to prevent custodial violence and torture during arrest and detention?
options: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal ((1997) 1 SCC 416)
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
Sunil Batra v. Delhi Administration (1980)
Rudul Sah v. State of Bihar (1983)
explanation: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal established 11 mandatory guidelines including identification tags, memo of arrest, right to inform friend/relative, medical inspection.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; D.K. Basu is the leading authority on arrest safeguards.

learningObjective: Master D.K. Basu arrest guidelines.

question: Under Section 47 BNSS (Section 50 CrPC), what information must the police officer arresting a person without warrant immediately communicate?
options: Full particulars of the offence for which he is arrested or other grounds for such arrest, and if offence is bailable, that he is entitled to be released on bail
Only the FIR number
The name of the informant
No information is required until production before Magistrate
explanation: Section 47 BNSS / S. 50 CrPC mandates communicating grounds of arrest immediately, and informing of right to bail if offence is bailable.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; grounds of arrest and right to bail.
optionBreakdown.D: Grounds must be given immediately at arrest.

learningObjective: Recall duty to inform grounds of arrest and bail eligibility.

question: Under Section 38 BNSS (Section 41D CrPC), an arrested person is entitled to meet an advocate of his choice:
options: During interrogation, though not throughout interrogation
Throughout interrogation continuously without interruption
Only after the police filing charge-sheet
Only after securing regular bail
explanation: Section 38 BNSS (Section 41D CrPC) provides that an arrested person is entitled to meet an advocate of his choice during interrogation, though not throughout interrogation.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; during interrogation, though not throughout.
optionBreakdown.B: 'Not throughout interrogation' is the statutory wording.

learningObjective: Recall right to consult advocate during interrogation.

question: What new institution is created under Section 37 BNSS (Section 41C CrPC) for public transparency of arrests?
options: Designated Police Officer in every district and at every police station, and display of names and addresses of all arrested persons on a digital portal / board
A national television channel for arrests
A military oversight council
An intelligence tribunal
explanation: Section 37 BNSS strengthens arrest transparency by establishing a designated police officer in every district and police station and displaying arrestee names digitally.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; designated officer and digital display of arrest information.

learningObjective: Identify arrest transparency reforms in BNSS S. 37.

question: In Pankaj Bansal v. Union of India ((2023) 16 SCC 1) and Prabir Purkayastha (2024), what did the Supreme Court hold regarding 'grounds of arrest'?
options: Written copy of grounds of arrest must be furnished to the arrestee as a matter of constitutional mandate under Article 22(1)
Oral intimation is sufficient in all cases
Grounds need only be revealed in the charge-sheet
Police have no duty to disclose grounds
explanation: Pankaj Bansal and Prabir Purkayastha mandated that written grounds of arrest must be served to enable effective exercise of right to legal counsel and bail.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; written copy of grounds of arrest is constitutionally mandatory.
optionBreakdown.B: Oral intimation held inadequate in Pankaj Bansal.

learningObjective: Master written grounds of arrest requirement.

question: Under Section 48 BNSS (Section 50A CrPC), the police officer making an arrest must immediately give information regarding such arrest and place of custody to:
options: Any friend, relative or other person disclosed or nominated by the arrested person
The local village pradhan only
The High Court Registrar
The media
explanation: Section 48 BNSS (Section 50A CrPC) mandates informing a nominated friend, relative, or person disclosed by the arrestee.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; nominated friend, relative or person disclosed.

learningObjective: Recall obligation to inform nominated person.

question: In Khatri (II) v. State of Bihar ((1981) 1 SCC 627) (Bhagalpur Blinding Case), what did the Supreme Court rule regarding legal aid for indigent accused?
options: State is under a constitutional mandate under Article 21 to provide free legal aid to an indigent accused from the moment of arrest and first production before Magistrate
Legal aid is only required at the Supreme Court stage
Accused must pay 50% of the legal aid costs
Magistrate has no duty to inform accused of free legal aid
explanation: Khatri held that the constitutional right to free legal aid attaches at the earliest moment of production before the Magistrate and Magistrate has a duty to inform accused.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; free legal aid from first production before Magistrate.
optionBreakdown.D: Magistrate has affirmative duty to inform.

learningObjective: Master right to free legal aid at first remand.

question: What is the legal effect if a police officer detains an arrested person beyond 24 hours without an order of a Magistrate under Section 167 CrPC / S. 187 BNSS?
options: The detention becomes illegal and unlawful, rendering the officer liable for wrongful confinement (S. 127 BNS) and civil damages for violation of Article 21
The detention automatically becomes valid if charge-sheet is filed later
No consequence if the offence was murder
The arrestee is permanently acquitted of all charges
explanation: Detention beyond 24 hours without a remand order constitutes illegal custody and wrongful confinement, entitling victim to habeas corpus and public law compensation.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; illegal custody, wrongful confinement, and Art 21 violation.
optionBreakdown.B: Subsequent charge-sheet does not cure prior illegal detention.
optionBreakdown.D: Does not automatically acquit, but custody is illegal.

learningObjective: Analyze consequences of violating 24-hour detention rule.

question: Under Section 54 BNSS (Section 55A CrPC), who has the statutory duty to take reasonable care of the health and safety of the accused while in custody?
options: The person having the custody of an accused
The accused's family members
The defence counsel
The High Court Bar Association
explanation: Section 54 BNSS (Section 55A CrPC) mandates: 'It shall be the duty of the person having the custody of an accused to take reasonable care of the health and safety of the accused.'

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; statutory duty of custodian to take reasonable care of health and safety.

learningObjective: Recall statutory duty of care of arrestee's health.

question: Under Section 63 BNSS (Section 61 CrPC), every summons issued by a court shall be:
options: In writing, in duplicate, signed by the presiding officer of such court or designated officer, and shall bear the seal of the court
Sent orally via police telephone
Published in a gazette only
Drafted and signed by the complainant
explanation: Section 63 BNSS (Section 61 CrPC) specifies form of summons: in writing, duplicate, signed by presiding officer, and bearing court seal.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; in writing, duplicate, signed, and sealed.
optionBreakdown.C: Gazette is for proclamation, not ordinary summons.

learningObjective: Recall form of summons.

question: What major reform does Section 64(2) BNSS introduce regarding the service of summons?
options: Explicitly authorizes service of summons in electronic form bearing digital signature or encrypted message via email, SMS or WhatsApp
Summons can only be delivered by physical horseback messenger
Electronic service is strictly banned
Electronic service applies only to government officers
explanation: Section 64(2) BNSS codifies modern electronic service: summons may be served in electronic form by email, messaging platforms or encrypted transmission.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; electronic service authorized under BNSS S. 64(2).

learningObjective: Master electronic service of summons in BNSS S. 64(2).

question: Under Section 72 BNSS (Section 70 CrPC), every warrant of arrest issued by a court shall remain in force until:
options: It is cancelled by the court which issued it, or until it is executed
The expiry of 6 months from the date of issue
The next general election
The retirement of the Magistrate
explanation: Section 72(2) BNSS (Section 70(2) CrPC) states: 'Every such warrant shall remain in force until it is cancelled by the court which issued it, or until it is executed.'

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; remains in force until executed or cancelled by court.
optionBreakdown.B: Does not lapse automatically by passage of time.
optionBreakdown.D: Judicial vacancies do not cancel warrants.

learningObjective: Master perpetual validity of warrant until executed/cancelled.

question: What is a 'Bailable Warrant' under Section 73 BNSS (Section 71 CrPC)?
options: A warrant with an endorsement by the court that if the person executes a bond with sufficient sureties, the officer shall release him from custody
A warrant that police can tear up if they like
A warrant issued only for witnesses
A summons disguised as warrant
explanation: Section 73 BNSS (Section 71 CrPC) provides for endorsement on warrant directing security to be taken; upon furnishing security, the arrestee is released.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; endorsed warrant with release on security.

learningObjective: Define bailable warrant.

question: Under Section 66 BNSS (Section 64 CrPC), if the person summoned cannot after the exercise of due diligence be found, summons may be served by leaving a duplicate for him with:
options: Some adult member of his family residing with him
A servant of the family
Any neighbour on the street
The postman
explanation: Section 66 BNSS (Section 64 CrPC) permits substituted service on some adult member of his family; Explanation clarifies a servant is not a member of the family.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; some adult member of his family.

learningObjective: Recall adult family member service rule.

question: In Inder Mohan Goswami v. State of Uttaranchal ((2007) 12 SCC 1), what did the Supreme Court hold regarding the issuance of non-bailable warrants (NBWs)?
options: Non-bailable warrants involve curtailment of liberty and should not be issued mechanically; courts should first issue summons, then bailable warrants, and NBWs only as a last resort
NBWs must be issued immediately upon non-appearance to any summons
Magistrates have unfettered discretion to issue NBWs
NBWs can only be issued in murder cases
explanation: Inder Mohan Goswami laid down that NBWs should not be issued mechanically where summons or bailable warrant would suffice, to balance individual liberty with administration of justice.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; NBW is a tool of last resort.
optionBreakdown.D: Can be issued across offences as last resort.

learningObjective: Master Inder Mohan Goswami NBW issuance guidelines.

question: Under Section 79 BNSS (Section 77 CrPC), where may a warrant of arrest be executed?
options: At any place in India
Only within the district of the issuing court
Only within the police station jurisdiction
Only within the State
explanation: Section 79 BNSS (Section 77 CrPC) provides: 'A warrant of arrest may be executed at any place in India.'

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; anywhere in India.

learningObjective: Recall territorial scope of warrant execution.

question: Under Section 67 BNSS (Section 65 CrPC), if service cannot by exercise of due diligence be effected under S. 64, 65 or 66, how may the summons be served?
options: By affixing one of the duplicates to some conspicuous part of the house or homestead in which the person summoned ordinarily resides
By publishing in a national newspaper
By radio broadcast
The case must be dropped
explanation: Section 67 BNSS (Section 65 CrPC) provides for affixing duplicate of summons to a conspicuous part of the house, followed by court inquiry.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; affixation on conspicuous part of house.
optionBreakdown.B: Newspaper is not the primary S. 65 method.

learningObjective: Recall service by affixation.

question: Under Section 74 BNSS (Section 72 CrPC), a warrant of arrest shall ordinarily be directed to:
options: One or more police officers, but the court may direct it to any other person if immediate execution is necessary
The complainant personally
The District Magistrate
The Army Commander
explanation: Section 74 BNSS (Section 72 CrPC) provides that a warrant is ordinarily directed to police officers, but court may direct to any other person if immediate execution is necessary.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; ordinarily to police officers, but may be to any person if necessary.
optionBreakdown.D: Military not involved in routine warrants.

learningObjective: Recall to whom warrants are directed.

question: What is the procedure under Section 77 BNSS (Section 75 CrPC) when a police officer executes a warrant of arrest?
options: Shall notify the substance thereof to the person to be arrested, and, if so required, shall show him the warrant
Must read the entire charge-sheet to the person
Must obtain signature of two gazetted officers
Can arrest silently without disclosing any warrant
explanation: Section 77 BNSS (Section 75 CrPC) requires notifying substance of warrant and showing it if required by the arrestee.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; notify substance and show warrant if required.
optionBreakdown.B: Charge-sheet not required at warrant execution.
optionBreakdown.D: Secret arrest without disclosing warrant is illegal.

learningObjective: Recall notification of substance of warrant.

question: Under Section 84(1) BNSS (Section 82(1) CrPC), what is the minimum statutory notice period that must be specified in a proclamation for an absconder?
options: Not less than thirty days from the date of publishing such proclamation
Not less than fifteen days
Not less than sixty days
Not less than seven days
explanation: Section 84(1) BNSS (Section 82(1) CrPC) mandates requiring the person to appear at a specified place and time not less than 30 days from date of publishing.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; not less than 30 days from publishing.

learningObjective: Recall 30-day notice period for proclamation.

question: What is the legal effect if the proclamation published under Section 82 CrPC / S. 84 BNSS gives less than 30 days to appear?
options: The proclamation is void ab initio and all consequential attachment proceedings under Section 83 CrPC / S. 85 BNSS are rendered completely illegal
It is a curable irregularity under Section 465 CrPC
It remains valid if approved by the Sessions Judge
The notice period is automatically extended by court staff
explanation: Devendra Singh Negi and consistent High Court rulings settle that giving less than 30 clear days violates the statutory mandate, vitiating the proclamation and subsequent attachment.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; void ab initio and vitiates attachment.
optionBreakdown.C: Sessions Judge cannot cure void proclamation.

learningObjective: Master mandatory 30-day requirement and nullity of defect.

question: Under Section 85(1) BNSS (Section 83(1) CrPC), when may the court order attachment of property of an absconding person?
options: At any time after the issue of proclamation, but simultaneously with proclamation if the court is satisfied that the person is about to dispose of or remove property from district
Only after 1 year from proclamation
Only after the accused is convicted in absentia
Immediately before issuing warrant of arrest
explanation: Attachment is ordered at any time after proclamation, but proviso allows simultaneous attachment if person is about to dispose of or remove property from local jurisdiction.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; after proclamation, or simultaneously if disposing of property.

learningObjective: Master timing of attachment of property.

question: Under Section 84(4) BNSS (Section 82(4) CrPC), for what offences may the court, after inquiry, pronounce an absconder as a 'Proclaimed Offender'?
options: Offences punishable with imprisonment of 10 years or more, imprisonment for life, or death penalty (such as murder, kidnapping for ransom, dacoity)
Any bailable offence
Traffic challans and fine defaults
Simple hurt only
explanation: Section 84(4) BNSS expands the list of heinous offences (punishable with 10+ years, life, or death) where court can declare the person a 'proclaimed offender'.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; heinous offences punishable with 10+ years, life, or death.
optionBreakdown.B: Cannot declare proclaimed offender in petty bailable cases.

learningObjective: Recall offences attracting Proclaimed Offender declaration.

question: What is the time limit under Section 86 BNSS (Section 84 CrPC) for making claims and objections to attachment of property by third parties?
options: Within six months from the date of the attachment
Within thirty days
Within three years
Within one year
explanation: Section 86(1) BNSS (Section 84(1) CrPC) provides that claims or objections must be preferred within six months from date of attachment.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; within six months from attachment.

learningObjective: Recall limitation period for third-party attachment claims.

question: If a claim or objection to attachment is disallowed under Section 86 BNSS (Section 84 CrPC), what remedy is available to the claimant?
options: May institute a civil suit within one year from date of disallowance to establish his right, subject to which the order shall be conclusive
Appeal directly to the Supreme Court
File an FIR against the Magistrate
No remedy exists
explanation: Section 86(4) BNSS / S. 84(4) CrPC enables the aggrieved claimant to institute a regular civil suit within one year to establish ownership right.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; civil suit within one year to establish property right.

learningObjective: Master civil suit remedy for disallowed attachment claims.

question: Under Section 87 BNSS (Section 85 CrPC), if the proclaimed person appears within the time specified in the proclamation:
options: The court shall make an order releasing the property from attachment
The property is automatically forfeited to the State
The property must be sold at auction immediately
The court must impose 50% property tax
explanation: Section 87(1) BNSS / S. 85(1) CrPC provides that if proclaimed person appears within time, court shall release property from attachment.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; court releases property from attachment.
optionBreakdown.B: Forfeiture occurs only if he fails to appear.
optionBreakdown.C: Sale is barred if he appears.

learningObjective: Recall release of property upon appearance.

question: Under Section 87(3) BNSS (Section 85(3) CrPC), within what period may an absconder appear and prove that he did not abscond to recover property or net proceeds of sale?
options: Within two years from the date of attachment
Within six months
Within five years
Within thirty days
explanation: Section 87(3) BNSS / S. 85(3) CrPC gives a two-year window from attachment for the person to prove absence was involuntary (no notice/could not attend).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; within two years from date of attachment.
optionBreakdown.B: Six months is for third-party claims.

learningObjective: Recall two-year window to reclaim attached property.

question: How is a proclamation published under Section 84(2) BNSS (Section 82(2) CrPC)?
options: Publicly read in some conspicuous place of town/village, affixed to conspicuous part of house, affixed to conspicuous part of court-house, and may also be published in daily newspaper
Only whispered to village pradhan
Sent by unsealed postcard
Posted on the High Court website only
explanation: Section 84(2) BNSS mandates threefold publication: public reading in town/village, affixation on house, affixation on court-house, and optional newspaper publication.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; public reading, house affixation, court affixation, and newspaper.

learningObjective: Recall statutory mode of publishing proclamation.

question: If the property attached consists of livestock or perishable articles, what may the court do under Section 85(2) BNSS (Section 83(2) CrPC)?
options: May direct immediate sale thereof, and the proceeds shall abide the result of the inquiry
Must keep animals without food until trial ends
Must release livestock unconditionally
Must deliver livestock to the complainant
explanation: Section 85(2) BNSS / S. 83(2) CrPC authorizes immediate sale of livestock or perishable property, with proceeds held in deposit.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; immediate sale of perishables/livestock.

learningObjective: Recall perishable property attachment rules.

question: Under Section 94 BNSS (Section 91 CrPC), who may issue a summons or written order to produce any document or other thing necessary for inquiry, trial or investigation?
options: Any Court or any officer in charge of a police station
Only the High Court
Only a Sessions Judge
The defence counsel
explanation: Section 94 BNSS (Section 91 CrPC) empowers either a Court (by summons) or an officer in charge of a police station (by written order) to require production.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; any Court or officer in charge of police station.
optionBreakdown.D: Defence counsel cannot issue statutory process.

learningObjective: Identify authorities empowered to issue process to produce documents.

question: In State of Gujarat v. Shyamlal Mohanlal Choksi (AIR 1965 SC 1251), what did the Constitution Bench hold regarding Section 91 CrPC (Section 94 BNSS)?
options: Section 91 CrPC does not apply to an accused person, because compelling an accused to produce incriminating documents violates Article 20(3) (protection against self-incrimination)
Section 91 applies equally to accused persons
Accused can be jailed for refusing to produce confession diary
Section 91 is unconstitutional
explanation: Shyamlal Mohanlal Choksi held that Section 91 CrPC cannot be used to compel an accused to produce self-incriminating documents in view of Article 20(3).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Section 91 does not apply to an accused person.
optionBreakdown.D: Provision is valid as applied to witnesses/others.

provision: BNSS S. 94 / CrPC S. 91 / Shyamlal Choksi (1965)
learningObjective: Master Shyamlal Choksi rule on S. 91 and Article 20(3).

question: Under Section 96 BNSS (Section 93 CrPC), when may a court issue a Search Warrant?
options: Where the court has reason to believe that a person will not produce the document on summons, or where it is not known who possesses it, or for general search/inspection
Whenever police request verbally
In all civil disputes
Only with consent of property owner
explanation: Section 96 BNSS (Section 93 CrPC) enumerates three conditions: (a) belief of non-compliance with S. 91; (b) possessor unknown; (c) general search/inspection necessary.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; three statutory grounds under S. 96 BNSS / S. 93 CrPC.
optionBreakdown.D: Search warrant overcomes lack of consent.

learningObjective: Recall conditions for issuing search warrant.

question: Under Section 96(3) BNSS (Section 93(3) CrPC), who alone can issue a search warrant for a document, parcel or thing in the custody of the postal or telegraph authority?
options: The District Magistrate or Chief Judicial Magistrate
Any Judicial Magistrate of the second class
Any Sub-Inspector of police
The Station House Officer
explanation: Section 96(3) BNSS / S. 93(3) CrPC restricts search warrants for postal/telegraph custody strictly to the District Magistrate or Chief Judicial Magistrate.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; District Magistrate or Chief Judicial Magistrate exclusively.

learningObjective: Master exclusive jurisdiction for postal search warrants.

question: Under Section 100 BNSS (Section 97 CrPC), when may a District Magistrate, SDM or Magistrate First Class issue a search warrant for persons wrongfully confined?
options: If there is reason to believe that any person is confined under such circumstances that the confinement amounts to an offence
Whenever a tenant fails to pay rent
Whenever a husband files for restitution of conjugal rights
Only after a civil decree is passed
explanation: Section 100 BNSS (Section 97 CrPC) provides a summary search warrant (quasi-habeas corpus) where a person is wrongfully confined amounting to an offence.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; search warrant for person wrongfully confined.

learningObjective: Define quasi-habeas corpus search warrant under S. 97 CrPC / S. 100 BNSS.

question: Under Section 103 BNSS (Section 100 CrPC), before making a search under this Chapter, the officer shall call upon:
options: Two or more independent and respectable inhabitants of the locality to attend and witness the search
Any two police constables
The accused's family members only
A magistrate personally
explanation: Section 103(4) BNSS / S. 100(4) CrPC mandates calling upon two or more independent and respectable inhabitants of the locality as search witnesses (panchas).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; two or more independent respectable locality inhabitants.
optionBreakdown.B: Police personnel cannot be independent panch witnesses.

learningObjective: Recall independent witness requirement for search (panchnama).

question: What groundbreaking technological requirement does Section 105 BNSS introduce regarding searches and seizures?
options: The process of conducting search of place or taking seizure of any property shall be recorded through audio-video electronic means, preferably by mobile phone
All searches must be broadcast on public television
Searches must be conducted using drone cameras only
Electronic recording is prohibited during searches
explanation: Section 105 BNSS is a monumental reform mandating mandatory audio-video electronic recording of searches and seizures and forwarding recording to Magistrate within 48 hours.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; mandatory audio-video electronic recording under Section 105 BNSS.

learningObjective: Master mandatory videography of search and seizure under BNSS S. 105.

question: Under Section 107 BNSS (Section 104 CrPC), what power does any Court have regarding documents or things produced before it?
options: May, if it thinks fit, impound any document or thing produced before it under this Sanhita
Must destroy the document after 7 days
Must return the document immediately without inspection
Can sell the document at market rate
explanation: Section 107 BNSS (Section 104 CrPC) provides: 'Any Court may, if it thinks fit, impound any document or thing produced before it under this Sanhita.'

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; court may impound document or thing produced.

learningObjective: Recall impounding powers under S. 104 CrPC / S. 107 BNSS.

question: Can a police officer conduct a search without a warrant under Section 185 BNSS (Section 165 CrPC)?
options: Yes, if he has reasonable grounds for believing that anything necessary for investigation cannot be otherwise obtained without undue delay, and records grounds in writing
No, warrantless search by police is void under all circumstances
Yes, without recording any reasons
Only in the presence of the Governor
explanation: Section 185 BNSS / S. 165 CrPC allows emergent search by IO without warrant, provided he records reasons in writing and specifies thing to be searched.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; emergent search permitted if reasons recorded in writing.
optionBreakdown.B: S. 165 is a recognized statutory exception.

learningObjective: Master police warrantless search under S. 165 CrPC / S. 185 BNSS.

question: In State of Maharashtra v. Natwarlal Damodardas Soni ((1980) 4 SCC 669), what was held regarding evidence obtained through an illegal search?
options: Illegality of search does not per se vitiate the trial or render the evidence inadmissible; court will only scrutinize evidence with greater care
Evidence obtained through illegal search is automatically excluded under Indian law
The accused must be discharged immediately
The investigating officer must be sentenced to 3 years imprisonment
explanation: Indian law follows the English doctrine: illegality of search does not render seized evidence inadmissible per se (Pooran Mal doctrine affirmed in Natwarlal).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; evidence remains admissible though scrutinized with greater care.
optionBreakdown.B: US exclusionary rule does not apply in India.

learningObjective: Analyze admissibility of evidence obtained through illegal search.

question: Under Section 126 BNSS (Section 106 CrPC), when a Court of Session or Magistrate First Class convicts a person of rioting, assault or offences involving breach of peace, what security may it demand?
options: Security for keeping the peace for a period not exceeding three years
Security for good behaviour for 7 years
Cash security of Rs 10 lakhs
Imprisonment in a labour camp
explanation: Section 126 BNSS (Section 106 CrPC) empowers the trial court upon conviction to order bond with or without sureties for keeping peace up to 3 years.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; security for keeping peace up to 3 years upon conviction.

learningObjective: Recall post-conviction security for keeping peace.

question: Under Section 127 BNSS (Section 107 CrPC), who may initiate preventive proceedings for Security for keeping the peace in other cases?
options: An Executive Magistrate, upon information that any person is likely to commit a breach of peace or disturb public tranquility
A Judicial Magistrate Second Class
The Chief Judicial Magistrate exclusively
The Superintendent of Police
explanation: Section 127 BNSS (Section 107 CrPC) confers jurisdiction on Executive Magistrates to take security for keeping peace up to 1 year.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Executive Magistrate upon information of likely breach of peace.

learningObjective: Recall jurisdiction for S. 107 preventive proceedings.

question: What is the maximum period for which security for keeping the peace may be required under Section 127 BNSS (Section 107 CrPC)?
options: Not exceeding one year
Not exceeding three years
Not exceeding six months
Not exceeding five years
explanation: Section 127(1) BNSS / S. 107(1) CrPC specifies that the bond shall be for a period not exceeding one year.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; not exceeding one year.
optionBreakdown.B: 3 years applies to S. 106 (on conviction) and S. 110 (habitual offenders).

learningObjective: Recall one-year limit for S. 107 peace bond.

question: Under Section 130 BNSS (Section 110 CrPC), security for good behaviour from habitual offenders may be demanded for a period not exceeding:
options: Three years
One year
Six months
Five years
explanation: Section 130 BNSS (Section 110 CrPC) empowers Executive Magistrates to require habitual offenders to execute a bond for good behaviour up to 3 years.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; not exceeding three years.

learningObjective: Recall three-year limit for habitual offender good behaviour bond.

question: In Madhu Limaye v. Sub-Divisional Magistrate ((1970) 3 SCC 746), what did the Supreme Court hold regarding Chapter VIII preventive proceedings (Sections 106–110 CrPC)?
options: Chapter VIII proceedings are constitutional and constitute reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2)-(5) in the interest of public order, but must comply strictly with natural justice
Chapter VIII is unconstitutional and violates fundamental rights
Magistrates can demand bonds without conducting any inquiry
Police can detain suspects indefinitely without Magistrate inquiry
explanation: Madhu Limaye Constitution Bench upheld the constitutional validity of Chapter VIII CrPC, ruling that preventive justice is distinct from punitive justice but requires fair hearing.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; constitutional reasonable restriction complying with fair procedure.
optionBreakdown.C: Inquiry is mandatory under S. 116 CrPC / S. 135 BNSS.

learningObjective: Master Madhu Limaye constitutional ruling on preventive bonds.

question: Under Section 135 BNSS (Section 116 CrPC), what is the maximum duration within which an inquiry under Chapter VIII must be completed?
options: Within six months from date of commencement, failing which the proceeding shall stand terminated unless extended for special reasons recorded in writing
Within thirty days
Within three years
No time limit exists
explanation: Section 135(6) BNSS / S. 116(6) CrPC mandates that inquiry shall be completed within six months, failing which it terminates automatically unless extended for special reasons.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; completed within six months or terminates automatically.

learningObjective: Master 6-month statutory inquiry termination rule.

question: Under Section 128 BNSS (Section 108 CrPC), security for good behaviour may be required from persons disseminating:
options: Seditious matters, matters promoting enmity between classes, or obscene matters
Lawful political criticism of municipal tax
Commercial advertisements
Scientific research papers
explanation: Section 128 BNSS (Section 108 CrPC) covers dissemination of matters punishable under BNS S. 152, 196, 197, or 294.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; matters endangering sovereignty, promoting enmity, or obscenity.

learningObjective: Recall scope of S. 108 CrPC / S. 128 BNSS.

question: Under Section 129 BNSS (Section 109 CrPC), security for good behaviour is taken from suspected persons who:
options: Are taking precautions to conceal their presence with a view to committing a cognizable offence
Are sleeping on a park bench peacefully
Are unemployed graduates
Have failed to pay their electricity bill
explanation: Section 129 BNSS (Section 109 CrPC) applies to persons taking precautions to conceal presence with a view to committing a cognizable offence (bond up to 1 year).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; concealing presence with view to committing cognizable offence.

learningObjective: Recall ingredients of S. 109 CrPC / S. 129 BNSS.

question: What is the consequence if a person ordered to give security under Section 106 or 117 CrPC (Section 126 or 136 BNSS) fails to give such security?
options: Shall be committed to prison until such period expires or until he gives security to the court
He shall be sentenced to 7 years rigorous imprisonment
He loses his Indian citizenship
His ancestral property is forfeited automatically
explanation: Section 141 BNSS (Section 122 CrPC) provides that failure to give security results in detention in prison until period expires or security is given.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; detention in prison until period expires or security given.
optionBreakdown.B: Substantive sentence of 7 years cannot be passed.

learningObjective: Recall detention consequences for failure to give security.

question: Can an order under Section 111 CrPC / Section 130 BNSS requiring an individual to show cause be issued without setting forth the substance of the information received?
options: No, the order must be in writing setting forth the substance of information received, amount of bond, term, and number/character of sureties
Yes, Magistrates can issue blank orders
Yes, police can fill in the details later
Information received must be kept permanently secret
explanation: Section 130 BNSS (Section 111 CrPC) mandates a written order setting forth substance of information, bond amount, period, and sureties to satisfy natural justice.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; substance of information and bond details mandatory.
optionBreakdown.B: Blank show cause orders are void.
optionBreakdown.C: Magistrate must draft and apply mind.

learningObjective: Master mandatory contents of show-cause order under S. 111 CrPC.

question: Which provision of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 corresponds to the famous Section 144 CrPC (urgent orders in cases of nuisance or apprehended danger)?
options: Section 163 BNSS
Section 144 BNSS
Section 187 BNSS
Section 223 BNSS
explanation: Section 163 BNSS corresponds directly to Section 144 CrPC.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Section 163 BNSS corresponds to Section 144 CrPC.
optionBreakdown.B: Section 144 BNSS corresponds to Section 125 CrPC (Maintenance).
optionBreakdown.C: Section 187 BNSS corresponds to Section 167 CrPC (Remand).
optionBreakdown.D: Section 223 BNSS is disobedience to public order.

learningObjective: Master statutory mapping: S. 144 CrPC is S. 163 BNSS.

question: What is the maximum initial validity period of an order passed by an Executive Magistrate under Section 163(4) BNSS (Section 144(4) CrPC)?
options: Not exceed two months from the making thereof
Not exceed six months
Not exceed fourteen days
One year
explanation: Section 163(4) BNSS (Section 144(4) CrPC) mandates that no order under this section shall remain in force for more than two months from the making thereof.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; maximum two months initially.
optionBreakdown.B: Six months is the maximum extension by State Government.

learningObjective: Recall 2-month initial validity period of S. 144 order.

question: Under the Proviso to Section 163(4) BNSS (Section 144(4) CrPC), the State Government may extend an order under this section for a further period not exceeding:
options: Six months from the date on which the order made by the Magistrate would have expired
Two years
One year
Indefinitely
explanation: The Proviso to Section 163(4) BNSS / S. 144(4) CrPC allows the State Government to extend the order for a maximum period not exceeding six months.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; State Government can extend up to six months.

provision: BNSS S. 163(4) Proviso / CrPC S. 144(4) Proviso
learningObjective: Recall 6-month maximum extension by State Government.

question: In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India ((2020) 3 SCC 637), what did the Supreme Court hold regarding the exercise of powers under Section 144 CrPC?
options: Power under Section 144 cannot be used to suppress legitimate expression of democratic rights; repetitive orders without material facts constitute abuse of power, and proportionality test must be satisfied
Section 144 orders are immune from judicial review
Internet shutdown orders under S. 144 can be indefinite
Magistrate has unfettered subjective discretion
explanation: Anuradha Bhasin established that S. 144 orders must satisfy the test of proportionality, cannot be repetitive or indefinite, and are subject to judicial review.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; proportionality test and bar on repetitive orders suppressing democratic rights.
optionBreakdown.D: Subjective satisfaction must be based on objective material.

learningObjective: Master Anuradha Bhasin ruling on S. 144 CrPC.

question: Can an order under Section 163 BNSS (Section 144 CrPC) be passed ex parte?
options: Yes, under subsection (2), in cases of emergency or in cases where circumstances do not admit of the serving of notice in due time
No, prior notice to all affected citizens is mandatory under all circumstances
Only if approved by High Court within 24 hours
Only during general elections
explanation: Section 163(2) BNSS / S. 144(2) CrPC explicitly permits ex parte orders in cases of emergency or where notice cannot be served in due time.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; ex parte order permitted in emergency.
optionBreakdown.B: Notice can be dispensed with in emergency.
optionBreakdown.C: HC approval not needed for ex parte order.

learningObjective: Recall emergency ex parte orders under S. 144 CrPC.

question: Under Section 163(1) BNSS (Section 144(1) CrPC), which of the following is NOT a legitimate objective for passing an order?
options: Suppressing peaceful political criticism of government policies
Preventing obstruction, annoyance or injury to any person lawfully employed
Preventing danger to human life, health or safety
Preventing a riot or an affray
explanation: Suppressing peaceful lawful dissent violates Article 19(1)(a) and is an illegal abuse of power outside Section 144 objectives.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; suppressing peaceful political criticism is illegal.

learningObjective: Identify statutory grounds for Section 144 orders.

question: Under Section 163(5)-(6) BNSS (Section 144(5)-(6) CrPC), what opportunity must be given to an aggrieved person who applies to rescind or alter an order?
options: The Magistrate or State Government shall afford him an earliest opportunity of showing cause or being heard
His application must be dismissed without hearing
He must deposit Rs 1 lakh fine before being heard
He must be detained under preventive detention
explanation: Section 163(5)-(6) BNSS / S. 144(5)-(6) CrPC mandates giving the applicant an earliest opportunity of showing cause, and recording reasons in writing if rejected.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; right to be heard and show cause at earliest opportunity.

learningObjective: Recall right of hearing against S. 144 order.

question: Can an order under Section 163 BNSS (Section 144 CrPC) be directed to the general public?
