options: Yes, under subsection (3), an order may be directed to a particular individual, or to persons residing in a particular place, or to the public generally when frequenting a particular place
No, must only be addressed to named individuals
Only to foreigners
Only to registered political parties
explanation: Section 163(3) BNSS / S. 144(3) CrPC explicitly states that order may be directed to public generally when frequenting or visiting a particular place.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; order can be directed to public generally frequenting a particular place.

learningObjective: Recall addressees of S. 144 orders.

question: In Babulal Parate v. State of Maharashtra (AIR 1961 SC 884), what did the Constitution Bench hold regarding the nature of power under Section 144 CrPC?
options: The power is preventive and intended to be used in anticipatory emergencies to prevent breaches of peace before they actually occur
Power can only be used after a riot has killed at least five people
Power is purely administrative and non-judicial
Section 144 was declared unconstitutional
explanation: Babulal Parate established that Section 144 is designed for preventive use in emergent situations to nip violence in the bud.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; preventive power intended for anticipatory emergencies.
optionBreakdown.B: Does not require waiting for bloodshed.

learningObjective: Analyze Babulal Parate precedent.

question: Disobedience to an order lawfully promulgated under Section 163 BNSS (Section 144 CrPC) is punishable under which section of BNS 2023?
options: Section 223 BNS (Section 188 IPC)
Section 152 BNS
Section 303 BNS
Section 106 BNS
explanation: Disobedience to an order under S. 163 BNSS / S. 144 CrPC is prosecuted under Section 223 BNS (Section 188 IPC).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; BNS Section 223 corresponds to IPC Section 188.

learningObjective: Identify penal section for violating Section 144 order.

question: Which provision of BNSS 2023 corresponds to Section 145 CrPC (procedure where dispute concerning land or water is likely to cause breach of peace)?
options: Section 164 BNSS
Section 145 BNSS
Section 168 BNSS
Section 173 BNSS
explanation: Section 164 BNSS corresponds directly to Section 145 CrPC.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Section 164 BNSS corresponds to Section 145 CrPC.

learningObjective: Map Section 145 CrPC to Section 164 BNSS.

question: What is the sole question to be decided by an Executive Magistrate under Section 164(4) BNSS (Section 145(4) CrPC)?
options: Which party was in actual possession of the subject-matter on the date of preliminary order, without reference to the merits of their claims to title
Who has the superior legal title and deed of ownership
Who paid more property taxes in the past 10 years
How the boundary should be permanently partitioned between heirs
explanation: Under Section 164(4) BNSS / S. 145(4) CrPC, the Magistrate decides only actual physical possession on date of preliminary order, completely detached from title.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; actual possession without reference to merits of title.
optionBreakdown.B: Title is exclusively for civil courts.
optionBreakdown.C: Tax records are evidential, not deciding issue.

learningObjective: Master core inquiry of Section 145 CrPC: possession vs title.

question: Under the Proviso to Section 164(4) BNSS (Section 145(4) CrPC), what is the statutory period for treating a forcibly and wrongfully dispossessed party as in possession?
options: If dispossessed within two months next before the date of the police report or other information received by the Magistrate
If dispossessed within six months
If dispossessed within one year
If dispossessed within 14 days
explanation: The Proviso creates a legal fiction: a party forcibly and wrongfully dispossessed within two months next before information received is treated as in possession on date of order.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; forcibly dispossessed within two months.
optionBreakdown.B: Six months is civil Specific Relief Act S. 6 period.

provision: BNSS S. 164(4) Proviso / CrPC S. 145(4) Proviso
learningObjective: Master two-month forcible dispossession rule under S. 145(4).

question: When can an Executive Magistrate attach the subject of dispute under Section 165(1) BNSS (Section 146(1) CrPC)?
options: In case of emergency, or if the Magistrate decides that none of the parties was in possession, or is unable to satisfy himself as to which was in possession
Whenever requested by the complainant without emergency
Whenever land value exceeds Rs 1 crore
Only after the civil court passes a decree
explanation: Section 165(1) BNSS (Section 146(1) CrPC) allows attachment in three situations: (1) case of emergency; (2) none in possession; (3) unable to decide possession.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; emergency, none in possession, or unable to satisfy who was in possession.

learningObjective: Recall three grounds for attachment under S. 146 CrPC / S. 165 BNSS.

question: In Ram Sumer Puri Mahant v. State of U.P. ((1985) 1 SCC 427), what did the Supreme Court hold regarding parallel Section 145 CrPC proceedings when a civil suit is pending?
options: When a civil suit is for the same property and the question of possession is involved and parties are in a position to approach civil court for interim injunction, parallel S. 145 proceedings should not be entertained
Section 145 CrPC always supersedes civil suits
Executive Magistrate can overrule civil court injunctions
Civil courts are barred from hearing land disputes
explanation: Ram Sumer Puri Mahant established that where civil court is already seized of question of possession/title, parallel S. 145 proceedings constitute abuse of process.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; civil suit takes precedence; parallel S. 145 proceedings deprecated.

provision: BNSS S. 164 / Ram Sumer Puri Mahant (1985)
learningObjective: Master Ram Sumer Puri rule on parallel civil suit and S. 145.

question: Under Section 164(5) BNSS (Section 145(5) CrPC), what must the Magistrate do if any party shows that no such dispute exists or has ceased to exist?
options: The Magistrate shall cancel the preliminary order, and all further proceedings thereon shall be stayed
The Magistrate must continue the proceedings to declare title
The Magistrate must sentence the parties to prison
The property must be auctioned
explanation: Section 164(5) BNSS / S. 145(5) CrPC mandates that if dispute likely to cause breach of peace ceases to exist, Magistrate shall cancel preliminary order and stay proceedings.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; cancel preliminary order and stay all further proceedings.

learningObjective: Recall cancellation of S. 145 proceedings when peace restored.

question: Under Section 166 BNSS (Section 147 CrPC), what disputes are investigated by an Executive Magistrate?
options: Disputes concerning the right of user of any land or water (e.g., easements, right of way, water flow) likely to cause breach of peace
Breach of commercial supply contracts
Disputes regarding copyright and patents
Disputes concerning defamation
explanation: Section 166 BNSS (Section 147 CrPC) covers disputes regarding the right of user of land or water (easements, access, water channels).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; right of user of land or water (easements/way).

learningObjective: Recall scope of S. 147 CrPC / S. 166 BNSS.

question: What is the nature of an order passed under Section 145 CrPC (Section 164 BNSS)?
options: It is an executive/police order maintaining status quo peace temporarily until rights are determined by a competent civil court
It is a final and conclusive judgment on title operating as res judicata in civil court
It creates an irrevocable partition of property
It transfers title to the State Government
explanation: An order under S. 145 CrPC is a police measure to maintain peace; it is subject to the determination of rights by a competent civil court (Bhinka v. Charan Singh).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; temporary status quo measure subject to civil court decree.
optionBreakdown.B: Does not operate as res judicata on title in civil court.

provision: BNSS S. 164 / Bhinka v. Charan Singh (1959)
learningObjective: Understand temporary police nature of S. 145 orders.

question: What happens to a receiver appointed by an Executive Magistrate under Section 165(2) BNSS (Section 146(2) CrPC) when a receiver is subsequently appointed by a civil court?
options: The magistrate's receiver shall be discharged and shall hand over possession to the receiver appointed by the civil court
The magistrate's receiver retains control over the civil court receiver
Both receivers manage the property jointly
The civil court appointment is void
explanation: Section 165(2) BNSS / S. 146(2) CrPC provides that upon civil court appointing a receiver, Magistrate's receiver shall be discharged and hand over possession.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Magistrate receiver discharged upon civil court appointing receiver.

learningObjective: Master superiority of civil receiver over magistrate receiver.

question: Does death of a party abate proceedings under Section 164 BNSS (Section 145 CrPC)?
options: No, under subsection (7), the legal representatives of the deceased party may be made parties to the proceeding and the inquiry shall continue
Yes, proceedings automatically abate completely
The land is automatically forfeited to the State
The surviving party is declared owner automatically
explanation: Section 164(7) BNSS / S. 145(7) CrPC states: 'Proceedings under this section shall not abate by reason only of the death of any of the parties; legal representatives can be substituted.'

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; proceedings do not abate; legal representatives substituted.

learningObjective: Recall non-abatement upon death of party under S. 145(7).
